title: Taiwan Builds Drone Hellscape, US Missile Stockpiles Crash 65%, Houthi Strike Hits Aramco Again
subhead: Taiwan's Han Kuang exercises showcase a new drone-centric defense doctrine targeting a Chinese invasion, while CSIS data reveals Patriot interceptor inventories have fallen by at least 65% since the Iran war began — and Houthis hit another Aramco refinery days after the Mecca Pact was signed.

sections.heading: Taiwan Unveils Drone 'Hellscape' Doctrine at Han Kuang Exercises
sections.body:
Taiwan's annual Han Kuang military exercises kicked off this week with a visible shift toward drone-centric warfare. Troops trained with reconnaissance and strike drones in central Taiwan as part of a 10-day exercise simulating a Chinese invasion, with reporters allowed to observe drone operations for the first time.

The 'hellscape' strategy — a term adopted from US military planners — envisions using mass drone swarms to detect, track, and attack an invading force across air, sea, and surface domains. Taiwan has established a new Littoral Combat Command integrating drones, mobile missiles, and artillery into a unified coastal defense structure. Lt Gen Huang Wen-chi, director general of strategic planning for Taiwan's defense ministry, acknowledged that drone efforts 'started relatively late' but said the approach has shifted substantially over the past two years.

The scale of ambition is significant: Taiwan's government has set a target of producing 100,000 drones per month by 2030, with about half intended for export. The military aims to acquire more than 210,000 aerial and maritime drones. A proposed $6.5 billion spending plan over five years has been blocked by opposition parties, who counter-proposed $7.4 billion over six years with requirements for increasing domestic production — a debate that mirrors wider disagreements over Taiwan's overall defense budget.

Taiwan exported $115 million worth of drones in the first quarter of 2026, already exceeding total 2025 exports, with the Czech Republic as the largest destination. Some Taiwanese drones are reportedly reaching Ukraine. Thunder Tiger and US defense firm Shield AI recently tested two sea-drone models designed to identify and attack enemy vessels.
sections.whyItMatters: Taiwan is moving from buying drones to building a domestic drone industrial base — and its export ambitions suggest it wants to become a global drone supplier, not just a consumer. The legislative budget fight, however, raises real questions about whether the hellscape concept can be funded fast enough to matter.

sections.heading: Patriot Interceptor Stockpiles Down 65% as Pentagon Demands Industry Acceleration
sections.body:
The Pentagon's push to accelerate weapons production is taking on sharper urgency. Deputy Defense Secretary Steve Feinberg sent a memo to defense industry leaders last week giving them 21 days to submit acceleration plans for 'significantly faster, more aggressive delivery schedules and/or increased production for critical capabilities,' according to a memo obtained by The Washington Post. 'Years-long development cycles are not acceptable,' Feinberg wrote.

New data from the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS) quantifies the severity. Patriot interceptor stockpiles have fallen from 2,330 before the Iran war to between 759 and 827 today — a decrease of at least 65%. THAAD interceptor inventories dropped from 452 pre-war to between 234 and 278, at least 38% below pre-war levels. CSIS warns that depleted inventories may force the US and its Middle Eastern allies to launch fewer interceptors, raising the risk of incoming Iranian drones and missiles getting through.

Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell confirmed the acceleration push is 'real' and said it will 'inform the fiscal year 2028 budget submitted to Congress for funding,' while insisting it is part of a broader modernization effort predating the Iran conflict. President Trump, meanwhile, posted on Truth Social denying any munitions shortage, claiming the US has 'massive amounts' and that 'large amounts are being manufactured and shipped to the U.S. as needed.'

A defense spending bill remains stalled in Congress, with lawmakers resisting a White House request to increase the budget to $1.5 trillion from about $900 billion last year.
sections.whyItMatters: The gap between the administration's public stance and the CSIS numbers is stark. If Patriot interceptors are truly below 827, the US faces a tangible readiness crisis — not just for the Iran conflict, but for any concurrent contingency in the Pacific or Europe.

sections.heading: Houthis Strike Aramco Jizan Refinery Days After Mecca Defense Pact
sections.body:
Yemen's Houthis claimed responsibility for a drone strike on Saudi Aramco's Jizan refinery on Sunday, two days after Saudi Arabia signed the Mecca Pact trilateral defense agreement with Turkey and Pakistan. A fire broke out at the facility and was later extinguished; no casualties were reported. The Saudi energy ministry confirmed the fire but did not attribute a cause.

Houthi military spokesperson Yahya Saree said the attack was launched in response to Saudi drone incursions into the Yemeni provinces of Saada and Hajjah. The group also claimed it had targeted Saudi troops and equipment in the Yemeni Red Sea port city of Mocha using 'a large number of ballistic missiles and drones.'

This is the second Houthi-claimed attack on the Jizan facility in a month, and follows earlier strikes on Aramco installations in Yanbu. Aramco CEO Amin Nasser said last week that attacks had caused some disruption but had not had 'a material operational or financial impact.' A separate explosion was also reported in the eastern Saudi city of Jubail, with local media reporting gas facilities had been targeted and caught fire.

The timing is pointed: the strike came 48 hours after the Mecca Pact was signed, underscoring that mutual defense commitments have not translated into improved air defense around Saudi energy infrastructure.
sections.whyItMatters: The Mecca Pact's credibility will be measured by whether it can protect Saudi territory. A drone reaching the Jizan refinery two days after a mutual defense pact was signed suggests the pact's practical deterrent value is, for now, limited.

sections.heading: Ukraine's AI Drone Race: $150 Autonomy Modules vs. Russian Camouflage
sections.body:
Ukraine is rapidly scaling AI-enabled strike drones as radio-controlled systems become 'largely obsolete' in heavily jammed environments. Former US Army Green Beret Bryan Pickens, who fought in Ukraine, told Forbes that autonomous systems have made strikes against Russian forces more effective: 'Anything radio-controlled is largely obsolete in those environments. Autonomous systems or satellite communications enabled systems are the future.'

Among the systems now in use is the Hornet, an AI-enabled fixed-wing strike drone produced by Perennial Autonomy, a US defense tech company founded by former Google CEO Eric Schmidt. It reportedly costs less than $10,000 per unit. Ukraine is also deploying the Darts drone with AI-guided targeting.

Ukrainian company The Fourth Law offers the TFL-1 autonomy module — available for as little as $150 — which can be installed on existing FPV drones to add AI targeting. Founder Yaroslav Azhnyuk claimed one brigade saw mission success rates increase from roughly 20% to 71% using the module, while expanding the effective kill zone from 3 km to 10 km, at a cost increase per drone of only about 10% (from ~$500 to ~$550).

Russia has begun adapting: Danylo Tsvok, head of Ukraine's Defense AI Center A1, said Russian forces are 'camouflaging equipment to deceive our drones' computer vision systems.' Ukraine has responded by retraining its AI models on new data showing the updated camouflage patterns.
sections.whyItMatters: The cost trajectory is remarkable — a $150 autonomy module that turns a $500 FPV drone into an AI-guided weapon achieving 71% mission success. This is the democratization of precision strike, and the countermeasure race (Russian camouflage vs. AI retraining) will shape the next phase of drone warfare globally.

sections.heading: BrahMos Becomes India's Defense Export Flagship After Combat Debut
sections.body:
India's BrahMos supersonic cruise missile is driving a defense export surge following its combat debut during Operation Sindoor in May 2025, when Indian Air Force Su-30MKI fighters fired at least 15 BrahMos missiles at Pakistani military installations from standoff ranges. The missile also demonstrated the ability to evade Chinese-origin air defense systems deployed by Pakistan.

The export momentum is tangible. Vietnam has concluded a deal believed to be worth $629 million, while Indonesia has finalized an agreement estimated at $200-300 million. The Philippines was the first customer, having signed a $375 million deal for three batteries in January 2022, with deliveries starting in April 2024. Malaysia and Thailand have also expressed interest.

Production is scaling to meet demand. BrahMos Aerospace now operates manufacturing facilities in Hyderabad, Nagpur, Pilani, and a newly commissioned plant in Lucknow, each capable of producing at least four missiles per month. India aims to raise annual defense exports to ₹50,000 crore (over $5 billion) within three years. The export-variant BrahMos has a range of 290 km, while the enhanced surface-to-surface variant may reach 800 km.

Notably, Russia — BrahMos's co-developer through NPO Mashinostroyeniya — has expressed interest in buying the missile for its own navy or ground forces, according to joint managing director Alexander Maksichev at the Fleet 2026 show in St Petersburg.
sections.whyItMatters: BrahMos is a rare case where a non-Western, non-Chinese weapon system is carving out real market share in Southeast Asia. If India can sustain this momentum, it creates a new pole in the global defense export landscape — one that offers competitive pricing, Indo-Russian provenance, and now combat credibility.

sections.heading: Royal Navy Increases Russia Patrols 25% as US Warns of NATO Hybrid Threats
sections.body:
The UK Ministry of Defence reported that Royal Navy deployments to monitor Russian warships and submarines in British waters have increased by 25% in the first seven months of 2026 compared with the same period in 2025. Royal Navy crews patrolled coastal and North Atlantic waters for 21 days in July alone.

The increase comes as US intelligence officials warn that Russia could carry out a limited land incursion or launch cyberattacks against NATO members as early as this autumn, with concerns stretching through 2029. A Russian missile landed in Poland last week, and an explosive drone was discovered at Leipzig Airport in Germany near a Ukrainian aircraft carrying weapons.

Poland's Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Radoslaw Sikorski said the US assessment reflected concerns that Putin could attempt a 'false flag' provocation, though he said Russia is 'not capable of launching an invasion of NATO.' Retired US Rear Admiral Mark Montgomery, director of the Foundation for Defence of Democracies, warned that Russia could employ 'new generation warfare' tactics including drone attacks, cyber operations, and disinformation campaigns to test NATO's response.

Meanwhile, Ukrainian President Zelensky announced a deal with the US for monthly deliveries of Patriot air-defense missiles.
sections.whyItMatters: A 25% increase in Royal Navy Russian-monitoring patrols is a concrete operational response to the intelligence warning, not just rhetoric. The combination of a missile in Poland, a drone at Leipzig, and the monthly Patriot commitment suggests a security environment where NATO's eastern and maritime flanks are both under pressure.

sections.heading: South Korea Designs Satellite-Drone Surveillance System Modeled on US-Iran Lessons
sections.body:
South Korean defense experts are pushing for a 'K-Composite Surveillance System' combining low-orbit satellite constellations with medium-altitude unmanned aerial vehicles (MUAVs), drawing directly on lessons from the US-Iran war. KAIST research associate professor Cho Sang-geun presented the concept at a National Assembly seminar on Thursday, noting that during Operation Epic Fury, drones flying around the clock filled a 30-minute surveillance gap left by satellites.

US Air Force Chief of Staff Gen. Kenneth Wilsbach told the House Armed Services Committee in May that 'the most valuable asset in Epic Fury was none other than the unmanned asset, the MQ-9.' The MQ-9 flew up to 12 orbits simultaneously over Iranian airspace for over 24 hours at a stretch, handling roughly 4,000 'dynamic targets' out of more than 13,000 strike targets. The US lost 42 aircraft and drones in the Iran war, 24 of them MQ-9 Reapers — but did not halt operations because 'a gap in the surveillance network was more fatal than losing a target.'

Korean Air rolled out the first production MUAV in April, with delivery to the Air Force scheduled for early next year. The drone has an approximately 90% domestic content rate, with subsystems from LIG D&A and Hanwha Systems. The concept envisions linking MUAVs with KF-21 fighters, Hyunmoo-5 missiles, and Aegis destroyers as 'motherships' in a manned-unmanned teaming combat system.
sections.whyItMatters: South Korea is institutionalizing Iran-war ISR lessons faster than most allies — and with a 90% domestic content rate on its strategic drone, it is deliberately reducing dependence on US platforms. If the K-Composite concept works, it becomes a template for other US allies looking to fill surveillance gaps without permanent American overhead.

bottomLine: Three stories dominated the defense landscape this weekend: Taiwan formally showcased a drone-centric defense doctrine targeting a Chinese invasion, with ambitions to produce 100,000 drones per month by 2030 and a domestic industry already exporting at record pace. The US acknowledged what CSIS data makes undeniable — Patriot interceptor stockpiles have dropped at least 65% since the Iran war began, and the Pentagon is giving industry 21 days to propose fixes. And Houthis hit another Aramco refinery just 48 hours after the Mecca Pact was signed, exposing the gap between defense declarations and defense reality. Meanwhile, Ukraine's $150 AI drone modules and India's BrahMos export surge show that the global defense market is being reshaped not just by great-power budgets, but by combat-proven, cost-effective systems from non-traditional suppliers.
sources: Forbes, New York Times, Times of India, Reuters, AP News, Middle East Eye, Strait Times, Outlook India, CNBC, Seeking Alpha, Business Standard, The Week, China Daily, PM News Nigeria, Herald Corporation Korea, MSN, Washington Post (via Outlook India/Arab Times), CSIS, CNBC
